title: On the Expressive Power of the Transverse-Field Ising Model for Graph Learning
abstract: We study the quantum evolution induced by graph-indexed Ising Hamiltonians as a source of structural signal for graph learning. Graph automorphisms preserve symmetries of the Hamiltonian, and these symmetries constrain the quantum evolution in a way that turns time-dependent local measurements into informative probes of graph structure. Leveraging this idea, we introduce QDAGer, a quantum-inspired graph-pair Transformer that injects quantum-dynamical features from time series of node occupations and connected two-point correlators directly into the attention mechanism. We apply QDAGer to learning Graph Edit Distance (GED), an NP-hard similarity measure, using either a direct permutation-invariant embedding discrepancy or an alignment-based surrogate loss. Experiments on multiple GED benchmarks under different edit cost settings show that the proposed dynamical features provide a stronger inductive bias than classical structural alternatives under the same training protocol. In addition, we report ablations where the dynamical signal is replaced by standard random-walk and heat-kernel features while keeping the architecture fixed, highlighting that the gain comes from the injected dynamics rather than model capacity alone.
summary: This paper proposes QDAGer, a quantum-inspired graph Transformer, to enhance graph learning by incorporating dynamical features derived from the Transverse-Field Ising Model. The authors show that the time evolution of quantum observables acts as a powerful structural signal, enabling the model to learn complex metrics like Graph Edit Distance better than purely classical structural descriptors.
main_problem: To develop graph representations for graph learning that capture structural information while respecting permutation invariance, particularly for hard tasks like graph comparison.
main_result: The proposed quantum-inspired architecture, QDAGer, demonstrates that dynamical features derived from the Ising model provide a stronger inductive bias for learning Graph Edit Distance than classical structural features.
method: The authors introduce QDAGer, a Transformer that injects time-series data from quantum observables (node occupations and two-point correlators) into the attention mechanism for graph-pair comparison.
model_or_system: The underlying physical model is the quantum evolution governed by a graph-indexed Transverse-Field Ising Hamiltonian ($H_G$). The dynamics are analyzed by measuring time-dependent expectation values of local observables.
important_parameters: The performance is tested across various Graph Edit Distance (GED) benchmarks using different edit cost settings.
main_assumptions: The quantum dynamics are simulated via emulation, and the method is positioned as 'quantum-inspired' rather than claiming quantum computational advantage.
figures_summary: Figure 1 (from Chunk 2 notes) shows that one-body occupation trajectories differ between non-isomorphic graphs (Rook's vs Shrikhande), demonstrating distinguishability.
paper_structure: The paper first establishes the theoretical distinguishability of non-isomorphic graphs using the Ising model dynamics (Chunks 2 & 3), proving that observables yield distinct time-dependent trajectories. It then applies this concept by proposing QDAGer, which integrates these dynamical features into a Transformer for practical graph learning tasks like GED (Chunks 1 & 4).
why_interesting: The work bridges quantum many-body physics (Ising models, dynamics) with modern machine learning (Graph Transformers), suggesting that inherent symmetries and time-evolution properties of quantum systems can serve as powerful, structured inductive biases for solving classically hard problems.
